title: Public Health Implications
section: From Clergy Wellness to Community Health
text:
From Clergy Wellness to Community Health
Faith leaders frequently occupy multiple roles within their communities, serving as spiritual guides, counselors, educators, advocates, and sources of social support.
These responsibilities create opportunities for faith leaders to influence community well-being. However, they also raise important questions about the resources, boundaries, and institutional support available to clergy themselves.
The Resilience in Leadership Initiative (RELI) Clergy Wellness Pilot offers an exploratory example of how physical wellness, spiritual development, and leadership support can be incorporated into a coordinated intervention.
The following implications are informed by the pilot’s survey findings, program activities, and descriptive Fitbit data.

title: Public Health Implications
section: 1. Clergy Wellness as an Occupational Health Concern
text:
1. Clergy Wellness as an Occupational Health Concern

Recognizing the Demands of Faith Leadership
Clergy responsibilities may extend beyond traditional working hours and include emotional support, crisis response, administrative leadership, and community engagement.
These responsibilities make occupational well-being an important consideration for faith-based organizations.
The RELI wellness assessments identified participant interests in physical health, mental wellness, work-life balance, supportive relationships, and spiritual development.
These findings suggest that clergy wellness initiatives should consider the multiple dimensions of health associated with professional and spiritual responsibilities.
Public Health Implication: Faith-based organizations can incorporate wellness resources, opportunities for rest, and professional support into their approaches to leadership development.

title: Public Health Implications
section: 2. Faith Institutions as Community Health Partners
text:
2. Faith Institutions as Community Health Partners

Connecting Spiritual Leadership and Public Health Practice
Faith institutions often provide opportunities for community connection, education, outreach, and social support.
Their existing relationships with congregants and community members may create opportunities for collaboration with public health professionals.
Potential activities include:

Community health education and prevention programming
Health screenings and referral partnerships
Mental health awareness and supportive conversations
Physical activity and nutrition initiatives
Connections to local health and social services

However, the capacity of faith institutions to implement these activities depends on available resources, organizational priorities, partnerships, and community needs.
Public Health Implication: Supporting clergy well-being may be an important component of building sustainable partnerships between faith institutions and public health organizations.

title: Public Health Implications
section: 3. Integrating Physical, Mental, and Spiritual Wellness
text:
3. Integrating Physical, Mental, and Spiritual Wellness

Moving Beyond Single-Domain Interventions
The RELI pilot combined physical wellness coaching, spiritual strategy and leadership coaching, and Fitbit-based activity monitoring.
This multidimensional approach recognized that clergy wellness cannot be understood solely through physical activity measurements.
Survey findings also highlighted interests in spiritual growth, mental wellness, supportive relationships, and professional development.
The Fitbit data offered descriptive information about recorded physical activity, but did not independently establish changes in overall health or well-being.
Public Health Implication: Future clergy wellness programs may benefit from integrating physical, emotional, social, and spiritual dimensions while evaluating each domain with appropriate measures.

title: Public Health Implications
text:
4. Program Accessibility, Engagement, and Sustainability

Reducing Barriers to Participation
The RELI pilot provided wellness resources, including Fitbit devices, athletic footwear, orthopedic support, and coaching opportunities.
These resources were intended to support engagement and address practical participation needs.
However, program participation varied. Five of seven participants completed movement sessions, while four of seven completed spiritual strategy sessions.
Variation in participation and wearable-device recording highlights the importance of accessible scheduling, communication, technical assistance, and ongoing engagement strategies.
Public Health Implication: Sustainable clergy wellness programs should consider participant availability, technology access, organizational support, and the resources needed to maintain participation over time.

title: Public Health Implications
section: 5. Recommendations for Future Public Health Evaluation
text:
5. Recommendations for Future Public Health Evaluation

Strengthening Measurement and Implementation
The RELI pilot provides a foundation for developing more structured approaches to evaluating clergy wellness initiatives.
Future evaluations should consider the following priorities:

Establish consistent baseline and follow-up measures. Use comparable assessments before and after participation to examine changes in wellness behaviors and self-reported outcomes.
Standardize wearable-data collection. Document device adherence, recording completeness, and participant monitoring periods before comparing activity outcomes.
Measure program engagement. Track attendance, coaching participation, resource utilization, and reasons for missed activities.
Include participant perspectives. Collect qualitative feedback about perceived benefits, barriers, and recommendations for improvement.
Assess longer-term sustainability. Explore whether wellness practices, organizational supports, and participant engagement continue after the intervention.
Expand evaluation when feasible. Larger participant groups and stronger study designs could help assess whether observed patterns are reproducible and whether program participation is associated with measurable improvements.

title: Public Health Implications
text:
Interpreting the Evidence Responsibly
The RELI Clergy Wellness Pilot was exploratory and involved a small participant group.
The wellness surveys included seven participants, while Fitbit-based physical activity analyses included six participants.
Differences in participation, recording completeness, and observation periods limit direct comparisons across individuals.
Furthermore, the descriptive findings do not establish that the intervention caused improvements in physical activity, health, or spiritual well-being.
The results should therefore be interpreted as preliminary evidence that can inform future program development and evaluation rather than definitive evidence of effectiveness.

title: Public Health Implications
text:
Conclusion: Beyond the Pulpit
Clergy are often expected to support the health and well-being of others, yet their own wellness needs may receive less structured attention.
The RELI pilot illustrates one approach to addressing these needs through coordinated physical wellness resources, spiritual development, leadership support, and activity monitoring.
For public health practitioners, the broader opportunity lies in developing partnerships that recognize faith leaders not only as community health partners, but also as individuals whose health deserves attention and investment.
Supporting the well-being of faith leaders is an opportunity to strengthen the relationship between faith, leadership, and public health practice.

title: The Intervention
text:
From Awareness to Action
This section introduces the RELI Clergy Wellness Initiative, including its program structure, wellness coaching, and strategies for supporting healthier faith leadership.

title: The Intervention
text:
Program Structure and Participant Incentives

Program Design
The RELI Clergy Wellness Pilot was designed as a 12–15-week initiative under the theme How to Have Your Healthiest Year Ever.
The program sought to equip participating clergy with practical strategies for maintaining physical, mental, and spiritual well-being during the holiday season and beyond.
The intervention incorporated three complementary components:

Physical wellness and performance coaching: Individualized guidance focused on movement, physical health, and sustainable wellness practices.
Spiritual strategy and leadership coaching: Support for personal reflection, vocational clarity, professional responsibilities, and spiritual well-being.
Wearable health monitoring: Fitbit devices used to record selected activity and wellness measurements over time.

Group sessions and individualized coaching opportunities also provided participants with avenues for accountability, support, and goal-setting.


Participant Incentives and Wellness Resources
The pilot incorporated tangible resources intended to support participation and reduce practical barriers to healthier behaviors.
These included:

Fitbit devices: Supported personal monitoring of activity and other available health measurements.
Athletic footwear: Gym shoes provided practical support for participation in physical activity.
Orthopedic support: Resources intended to accommodate individual physical wellness needs.
Coaching access: Opportunities for personalized wellness and spiritual development guidance.

These resources represented program participation supports rather than documented financial incentives or performance-based rewards.


Program Participation and Engagement
Program participation varied across intervention components.
Five of seven participants completed movement sessions with the wellness and performance coach, while four of seven completed spiritual strategy sessions.
The evaluation also identified opportunities to strengthen engagement through improved communication, routine check-ins, technical assistance, and more consistent attendance.


Implications for Program Evaluation
The combination of coaching, tangible wellness resources, and wearable monitoring created opportunities to examine clergy wellness from multiple perspectives.
However, participation differences, device adherence, and varying levels of engagement must be considered when interpreting recorded outcomes.
Because the pilot did not isolate the effects of individual components, observed changes cannot be attributed specifically to Fitbit use, coaching, or participant incentives.

Who Cares for the Caregivers?
Clergy are often expected to provide emotional, spiritual, and community support while navigating significant responsibilities of their own.
Beyond the Pulpit explores the health and wellness of faith leaders through public health evaluation, data visualization, and the RELI Clergy Wellness Initiative.

title: Home
text:
The Public Health Problem
Clergy frequently balance demanding ministry responsibilities with personal, family, and community obligations. These competing demands may create challenges related to:

Physical activity and healthy lifestyle behaviors
Sleep quality and adequate rest
Stress management and emotional well-being
Work-life balance
Access to structured wellness support

Understanding these challenges is an important step toward developing effective and sustainable wellness initiatives.

text:
Understanding the Health of Faith Leader
Clergy are often expected to provide emotional, spiritual, and community support while navigating significant responsibilities of their own.
This section examines the physical, emotional, and spiritual wellness needs of faith leaders, including the challenges of balancing ministry responsibilities with personal health.

title: Clergy Wellness
text:
Areas of Focus

Physical health and wellness behaviors
Sleep quality and rest
Emotional well-being and stress
Work-life balance and self-care
Access to wellness resources

title: Clergy Wellness
text:
Why Clergy Wellness Matters
Supporting clergy wellness is an important consideration for faith-based organizations and public health practitioners. Understanding the needs of faith leaders can inform programs that promote healthier and more sustainable ministry.

title: Clergy Wellness
text:
Understanding Holistic Clergy Wellness
Faith leaders occupy a unique position at the intersection of spiritual leadership, community service, and personal responsibility. Beyond providing religious instruction, clergy frequently serve as counselors, advocates, organizational leaders, and sources of emotional support for individuals experiencing personal or community challenges.
While these responsibilities can provide a strong sense of purpose and fulfillment, they may also create competing demands on clergy members’ physical health, emotional well-being, and spiritual development.
Clergy wellness must therefore be understood as a multidimensional public health concern. Physical health influences an individual’s capacity to maintain daily activities, manage occupational demands, and sustain healthy behaviors. Spiritual wellness, meanwhile, encompasses dimensions of meaning, purpose, personal growth, and the relationship between religious identity and well-being.
These dimensions are interconnected. A clergy member may experience strong spiritual fulfillment while simultaneously struggling with inadequate sleep, limited physical activity, or difficulty establishing boundaries between ministry and personal life.
Understanding these experiences requires an evaluation approach that considers both measurable health behaviors and the broader personal and professional circumstances influencing them.

title: Clergy Wellness
text:
Two Surveys, Two Perspectives
The RELI Clergy Wellness Pilot incorporated two complementary survey instruments to explore different dimensions of participants’ well-being.

title: Clergy Wellness
section: Total Body Wellness Survey: Understanding Physical Health
text:
Total Body Wellness Survey: Understanding Physical Health
The Total Body Wellness Survey examined participants’ physical health, wellness behaviors, and related health concerns.
Its questions addressed areas such as physical activity, sleep, discomfort, emotional health, and other factors that may influence overall wellness.
From a public health perspective, this instrument helped establish a baseline understanding of participants’ health behaviors and potential areas of concern. These findings provide context for understanding why physical wellness education, activity monitoring, and individualized support may be valuable components of clergy wellness programming.

Part I: Physical Health and Wellness



Total Body Wellness and Performance Survey




Understanding Physical Wellness Among Clergy
The Total Body Wellness and Performance Survey was designed to assess the physical health, lifestyle behaviors, and wellness needs of clergy participating in the RELI pilot program.
The survey examined several dimensions of health, including sleep, physical activity, emotional well-being, and physical discomfort.
These measures are significant because the demands of ministry may influence clergy members’ opportunities to prioritize rest, exercise, and preventive health practices.


Key Physical Health Findings
The baseline survey included seven clergy participants, with an average reported age of 55.3 years.
The findings highlighted several areas relevant to physical wellness:

Sleep: Six of seven participants reported sleeping approximately five to seven hours per night.
Physical activity: Four of seven reported exercising three to five days per week.
Emotional health: Three participants reported some level of anxiety.
Physical discomfort: Three participants reported neck discomfort.

These findings provide a descriptive picture of selected health concerns and behaviors within the pilot cohort.


Visualizing Physical Wellness








Figure 1: Reported nightly sleep duration among RELI clergy participants (n = 7).







Interpreting Sleep Patterns
Six of the seven participants (85.7%) reported sleeping approximately five to seven hours per night, while one participant (14.3%) reported sleeping fewer than five hours.
These findings suggest that sleep duration is an important consideration for clergy wellness programming. All seven participants reported sleep durations below the seven to nine hours generally recommended for adults in this age group.
Although the survey does not establish the reasons for these patterns, occupational demands, stress, and competing personal responsibilities may be relevant factors for future investigation.
These baseline findings provide context for examining Fitbit-derived sleep measurements during the RELI intervention, including whether objectively recorded sleep patterns align with participants’ self-reported experiences.


Physical Activity Frequency








Figure 2: Weekly physical activity frequency among RELI clergy participants (n = 7).







Interpreting Physical Activity Patterns
Four of the seven participants (57.1%) reported engaging in at least 30 minutes of physical activity on three to five days per week. Two participants (28.6%) reported being active two days per week, while one response was recorded as not applicable (14.3%).
These findings indicate variation in reported physical activity frequency within the cohort. Although most participants reported some regular activity, the survey did not establish whether their activity levels consistently met recommended weekly physical activity guidelines.
From a public health perspective, these baseline findings highlight an opportunity to support sustainable physical activity habits through individualized wellness coaching and monitoring.
The survey results also provide context for examining changes in Fitbit-derived steps and active-zone minutes during the RELI intervention.


Physical Discomfort and Mobility








Figure 3: Reported areas of physical discomfort among RELI clergy participants (n = 7). Multiple responses permitted.







Interpreting Physical Discomfort
The Total Body Wellness and Performance Survey identified several areas of self-reported physical discomfort among the seven participating clergy members. Neck and hip discomfort were the most frequently reported concerns, each identified by three participants (42.9%). Shoulder discomfort was reported by two participants (28.6%), while knee and ankle discomfort were each reported by one participant (14.3%).
Two participants reported no discomfort in the assessed areas. Because respondents could identify multiple areas of discomfort, the reported frequencies are not mutually exclusive.
These findings suggest that physical wellness programming may benefit from incorporating mobility, flexibility, and individualized approaches to physical activity. However, the survey does not establish the severity, duration, or clinical causes of the reported discomfort.
From a public health perspective, understanding physical limitations is important when interpreting participants’ activity levels and designing appropriate wellness interventions. Such considerations may also help contextualize differences in Fitbit-derived activity measurements during the RELI pilot.


Emotional Wellness and Anxiety
Although the Total Body Wellness and Performance Survey primarily examined physical health behaviors, it also assessed participants’ experiences with anxiety.
Four of the seven clergy participants (57.1%) reported experiencing no anxiety. The remaining three participants (42.9%) reported varying levels of anxiety, with one participant each selecting levels 1, 3, and 4 on a five-point scale.
These findings suggest that emotional wellness deserves consideration alongside physical activity, sleep, and mobility. While most participants did not report anxiety, the variation in responses highlights the importance of recognizing individual differences in emotional well-being.
From a public health perspective, emotional wellness may be influenced by multiple factors, including occupational responsibilities, social support, personal circumstances, and access to appropriate mental health resources. However, the survey does not establish the underlying causes of participants’ reported anxiety.
The findings reinforce the value of a holistic approach to clergy wellness that considers both physical and emotional health, rather than treating them as separate concerns.


Public Health Interpretation
The findings suggest that clergy wellness programming may benefit from addressing multiple health dimensions rather than focusing exclusively on exercise.
Sleep, physical discomfort, and emotional well-being may influence an individual’s ability to maintain consistent physical activity and self-care routines.
However, the small sample size limits generalizability, and the survey findings do not establish that ministry responsibilities caused the reported health concerns.


From Physical Health to Ministerial Wellness
The Total Body Wellness and Performance Survey identified several health-related considerations among participating clergy, including sleep duration, physical activity, musculoskeletal discomfort, and emotional well-being.
However, understanding these health indicators requires consideration of the broader circumstances in which clergy live and work.
Faith leaders often navigate competing responsibilities involving congregational care, organizational leadership, community engagement, and personal relationships. These responsibilities may influence the time, resources, and support available for maintaining healthy routines.
The Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey provides an opportunity to examine these broader experiences, including barriers to self-care, leadership development needs, and the role of spiritual and professional support.
Together, these findings help connect individual wellness behaviors with the organizational and interpersonal dimensions of clergy health.

title: Clergy Wellness
section: Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey: Understanding Spiritual and Ministerial Well-Being
text:
Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey: Understanding Spiritual and Ministerial Well-Being
The Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey explored participants’ experiences with ministry responsibilities, self-care, leadership development, coaching, and personal or spiritual growth.
Unlike the Total Body Wellness Survey, which emphasized health behaviors and conditions, this instrument provided insight into the professional and personal circumstances surrounding clergy wellness.
The survey addressed challenges such as competing responsibilities, time management, work-life balance, and access to supportive relationships.
These areas are particularly relevant to public health because wellness behaviors do not occur in isolation. An individual’s ability to prioritize health may be influenced by organizational expectations, occupational demands, available resources, and social support.

Part II: Spiritual and Ministerial Wellness



Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey




Understanding the Demands of Ministry
The Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey examined the personal, professional, and spiritual dimensions of clergy well-being.
While the Total Body Wellness Survey emphasized health behaviors and physical wellness, this instrument explored the responsibilities and experiences that may influence clergy members’ ability to maintain healthy routines.


Key Areas of Investigation
The survey explored:

Time management and boundary-setting
Work-life balance and self-care
Leadership development and professional responsibilities
Coaching, mentorship, and peer support
Spiritual renewal and personal growth



Barriers to Maintaining Self-Care








Figure 4: Anticipated barriers to maintaining self-care routines among RELI clergy participants (n = 7). Multiple responses permitted.







Interpreting Barriers to Self-Care
The Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey identified several anticipated challenges to maintaining consistent self-care routines among participating clergy. Lack of time was the most frequently reported barrier, selected by six of seven participants (85.7%), followed by difficulty setting boundaries, identified by four participants (57.1%).
Three participants (42.9%) identified a lack of supportive networks, while one participant (14.3%) selected ministry-related stress. Because respondents could select multiple barriers, these categories are not mutually exclusive.
These findings highlight the relationship between personal wellness and the broader responsibilities associated with ministry. Although clergy may recognize the importance of self-care, competing demands and limited support can create challenges in maintaining consistent wellness practices.
From a public health perspective, these findings suggest that clergy wellness initiatives should extend beyond individual health education to consider organizational expectations, boundary-setting, time management, and supportive relationships.
The findings provide a rationale for incorporating leadership coaching, peer support, and individualized wellness planning into faith-based health promotion initiatives.


Self-Care Priorities Among Clergy








Figure 5: Self-care practices RELI clergy participants wanted to prioritize over the next six months (n = 7). Multiple responses permitted.







Interpreting Clergy Wellness Priorities
All seven participants (100%) identified spiritual health, including prayer, meditation, and reflection, as a self-care priority for the following six months.
Physical health, mental health, and building supportive relationships were each selected by six participants (85.7%). Two participants (28.6%) identified additional priorities outside these categories.
These findings suggest that participating clergy viewed wellness as a multidimensional concern encompassing spiritual, physical, psychological, and social well-being.
Importantly, the emphasis on spiritual health did not exclude interest in other forms of self-care. Instead, participants expressed overlapping priorities, highlighting opportunities to integrate conventional health promotion strategies with practices already valued within faith communities.
When considered alongside the previously reported barriers to self-care, these findings reveal a potential gap between wellness intentions and the practical ability to maintain healthy routines.
For faith-based public health programming, this distinction is significant. Effective interventions may benefit from addressing the organizational and personal barriers that prevent clergy from translating their wellness priorities into sustainable behaviors.


Spiritual Aspirations and Leadership Development








Figure 6: Spiritual aspirations reported by RELI clergy participants (n = 7). Multiple responses permitted.







Interpreting Spiritual Aspirations
The Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey revealed a strong interest in spiritual development among participating faith leaders.
All seven participants (100%) identified strengthening spiritual leadership as an aspiration. Five participants (71.4%) expressed a desire to cultivate greater joy and peace in ministry, while four participants (57.1%) prioritized deepening their personal faith. Three participants (42.9%) identified finding clarity in their vocational purpose as an important goal.
These findings suggest that participants’ aspirations extended beyond professional effectiveness to include personal fulfillment, spiritual renewal, and a more sustainable relationship with ministry.
The emphasis on cultivating joy and peace is particularly relevant when considered alongside previously identified challenges involving time constraints, boundary-setting, and self-care.
From a public health perspective, spiritual wellness may serve as a meaningful component of broader health promotion initiatives in faith-based settings. Integrating spiritual development with practical wellness strategies may help align programming with participants’ stated priorities.
However, these baseline responses represent participants’ aspirations rather than demonstrated improvements in spiritual well-being or leadership effectiveness.


Professional Development Priorities








Figure 7: Professional development priorities among RELI clergy participants (n = 7). Multiple responses permitted.







Interpreting Professional Development Needs
The Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey identified several professional development priorities among participating faith leaders.
Work-life balance strategies emerged as the most frequently selected area, identified by six of seven participants (85.7%). Five participants (71.4%) expressed interest in strengthening leadership and administrative skills, while four participants (57.1%) prioritized conflict resolution. Three participants (42.9%) selected preaching and teaching, and one participant (14.3%) identified an additional area of professional development.
These findings suggest that participating clergy viewed professional development as extending beyond traditional ministerial responsibilities. Their interests included practical skills for managing competing demands, navigating interpersonal challenges, and maintaining sustainable leadership practices.
The emphasis on work-life balance is particularly significant when considered alongside previously reported difficulties with time management and boundary-setting. Together, these responses suggest that clergy recognize a need for strategies that support both professional effectiveness and personal well-being.
From a public health perspective, leadership development may complement wellness programming by addressing organizational and occupational conditions that influence self-care. Training in delegation, communication, conflict resolution, and boundary-setting could help create more supportive environments for clergy health.
These findings provide a rationale for integrating professional coaching with physical and spiritual wellness initiatives, although the survey does not establish whether these approaches improved participant outcomes.


Understanding the Findings
The survey findings will be examined through a combination of quantitative figures and qualitative thematic analysis.
Particular attention will be given to barriers to self-care, challenges associated with ministry responsibilities, and the role of supportive relationships in promoting wellness.


Public Health Interpretation
Clergy wellness is influenced not only by personal health behaviors but also by occupational expectations, social support, and organizational conditions.
These findings provide an opportunity to consider how faith-based institutions can support clergy through policies, resources, and leadership practices that promote sustainable ministry.


Why Both Surveys Matter
Together, the two instruments provide a more comprehensive picture of clergy wellness.
The Total Body Wellness Survey helps identify what health behaviors and concerns are present, while the Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey provides insight into the responsibilities, experiences, and support needs that may influence those behaviors.
This distinction is important because identifying a health concern does not necessarily explain the circumstances contributing to it.
For example, limited sleep may be identified through a physical wellness assessment, while information about ministry demands and difficulty maintaining boundaries can provide additional context for interpreting that concern.

title: Clergy Wellness
text:
Qualitative Findings: Voices of Clergy
While quantitative survey responses identified common wellness priorities and barriers, open-ended responses provided additional insight into participants’ personal experiences, expectations, and desired outcomes.
The following themes were identified through a descriptive review of responses to the Outcome-Focused Clergy Wellness Survey.

Theme 1: Accountability and Support
Participants identified accountability, encouragement, and shared experiences as valuable aspects of group coaching.
Responses emphasized the importance of supportive relationships, opportunities to exchange personal experiences, and encouragement from others navigating similar ministerial responsibilities.
These findings suggest that peer connection may be an important component of clergy wellness programming.


Theme 2: Boundary-Setting and Time Management
Participants identified boundary-setting, time management, and self-reflection as challenges in pursuing their personal and professional goals.
Responses also highlighted interest in distinguishing meaningful self-care from superficial wellness practices.
These concerns reinforce the quantitative findings identifying limited time and difficulty establishing boundaries as common barriers to self-care.


Theme 3: Vocational Clarity and Personal Growth
Participants expressed a desire for greater clarity regarding their professional, personal, and ministerial calling.
Desired outcomes included setting realistic goals, strengthening consistency in personal wellness routines, and reducing feelings of anxiety and hurry.
These responses illustrate how clergy wellness extends beyond physical health to include purpose, emotional well-being, and sustainable leadership.


Theme 4: Individualized Coaching and Goal Achievement
When asked about one-on-one coaching, participants expressed interest in personalized goal-setting, motivation, accountability, new perspectives, and practical support.
Their responses suggest that individualized coaching may complement group programming by allowing participants to address their specific goals and challenges.


Qualitative Interpretation
Taken together, these themes suggest that participating clergy sought more than information about healthy behaviors. Their responses emphasized the importance of practical strategies, supportive relationships, personal reflection, and individualized guidance.
The qualitative findings also complement the quantitative survey results by illustrating how professional responsibilities, spiritual aspirations, and personal wellness needs intersect.
These themes represent a descriptive synthesis of the reported responses rather than a formal qualitative coding analysis. The small cohort size and limited response detail should be considered when interpreting the findings.
Although the surveys do not establish causal relationships between these factors, examining their findings together can help identify opportunities for more responsive wellness programming.
The RELI evaluation therefore approaches clergy wellness not simply as a matter of individual health choices, but as an issue shaped by the interaction of personal behaviors, professional responsibilities, spiritual identity, and institutional support.

title: Program Outcomes
text:
What the Data Reveal
This section presents descriptive findings from the Resilience in Leadership Initiative (RELI) Clergy Wellness Pilot, including Fitbit-derived physical activity outcomes. The pilot also incorporated wellness assessments and spiritual leadership development, discussed elsewhere on this website.
The visualizations below were developed in RStudio to examine recorded activity patterns across six participants from November 2024 through February 2025.

title: Program Outcomes
text:
Fitbit-Derived Physical Activity Outcomes

Monthly Active Zone Minutes








Figure 1: Recorded monthly Active Zone Minutes among six RELI participants, November 2024–February 2025.







Interpreting Activity Patterns
Recorded Active Zone Minutes varied substantially across participants and months.
Several participants recorded higher totals in December than in November, while others continued to increase into January or February. These patterns indicate that recorded activity trajectories were not uniform across the pilot cohort.
However, monthly totals may be influenced by differences in Fitbit onboarding, device wear, recording completeness, and the number of days represented within each month.
These findings are descriptive and should not be interpreted as evidence that the intervention independently caused changes in physical activity.


Monthly Step Counts








Figure 2: Average daily recorded steps by participant and month, November 2024–February 2025.







Interpretation of Monthly Step Counts
Average daily recorded steps varied across participants throughout the RELI Clergy Wellness Pilot. The observed patterns suggest substantial individual variation in recorded physical activity during the observation period.
The number of days with Fitbit step-count records also differed across participants, ranging from 66 to 105 days.
These differences may reflect variation in device use, onboarding dates, recording completeness, or participants’ activity patterns. Days containing only partial recordings were not independently validated as complete device-wear days.
Consequently, these averages should be interpreted as descriptive measures of available recorded activity rather than definitive estimates of participants’ total daily physical activity.

title: Program Outcomes
text:
Baseline and Follow-Up Physical Activity








Figure 3: Average recorded daily steps during the first and last 30 calendar days of available Fitbit data for each participant.






Interpreting Baseline and Follow-Up Patterns
The comparison of the first and last 30 calendar days of available Fitbit records reveals differences in recorded daily step averages across participants.
Some participants demonstrated higher average recorded steps during their final observation window, while others showed lower averages. These mixed patterns indicate that changes in recorded activity were not consistent across all six participants.
Importantly, these periods represent the beginning and end of each participant’s available Fitbit data, rather than standardized pre-intervention and post-intervention assessments.
Differences in recording completeness, seasonal conditions, participant schedules, and device use may influence the observed comparisons.
Therefore, the figure should be understood as an exploratory comparison of recorded activity patterns, not as a causal estimate of intervention effectiveness.

title: Program Outcomes
text:
Public Health Interpretation
The RELI pilot demonstrates the potential value of incorporating wearable activity monitoring into faith-centered wellness programming.
Fitbit records provide an opportunity to describe physical activity patterns over time, complementing participants’ self-reported wellness priorities and experiences.
However, the findings also highlight the importance of consistent device use, standardized observation periods, and clear procedures for evaluating data completeness.
Future RELI evaluations could strengthen physical activity measurement by establishing minimum recording-day criteria, monitoring device adherence, and comparing equivalent observation periods.
Taken together, these findings support continued exploration of integrated wellness approaches that address the physical, spiritual, and professional responsibilities of faith leaders.

title: Program Outcomes
text:
Evaluation Limitations
This analysis has several important limitations:

Small sample: Fitbit activity records were available for six participants.
Incomplete recordings: Recorded days may not represent complete 24-hour activity measurements.
Unequal observation periods: Participants began and ended recording on different dates.
Descriptive design: No comparison group or standardized causal evaluation was available.
Measurement differences: Monthly Active Zone Minutes and daily step counts capture different dimensions of physical activity.

These limitations should inform the interpretation of findings and the design of future RELI evaluations.

title: About the Initiative
section: About the Resilience in Leadership Initiative
text:
About the Resilience in Leadership Initiative
The Resilience in Leadership Initiative (RELI) at Chicago Theological Seminary (CTS) supports clergy, ministers, lay leaders, and seminary students who serve historically marginalized and disenfranchised communities.
Through mentorship, leadership development, peer relationships, and wellness-focused programming, RELI seeks to strengthen vocational resilience and promote sustainable ministry.
The initiative recognizes that faith leaders serve as spiritual guides, community advocates, and sources of emotional support. Sustaining these responsibilities requires attention not only to professional development, but also to personal health and well-being.

The Clergy Wellness Pilot
Supported through CTS’s Thriving in Ministry programming, the RELI Clergy Wellness Pilot brought together expertise in pastoral leadership, spiritual formation, physical wellness, public health, and technology.
The pilot was designed to explore a more holistic approach to supporting clergy wellness, recognizing the connections among physical health, emotional resilience, spiritual renewal, and leadership sustainability.
This website examines that work through a public health and data visualization lens.

title: About the Initiative
text:
Meet the Team
The initiative benefited from a multidisciplinary team whose expertise spans faith leadership, coaching, wellness, technology, and public health evaluation.



Rev. Dr. Brian E. Smith, Program Convenor and Director


Rev. Dr. Brian E. Smith, DMin, MHSA, MDiv, is a faith leader, community partnership strategist, and the Program Convenor and Director of the RELI Clergy Wellness Initiative.
Through his work at Chicago Theological Seminary, Dr. Smith has supported initiatives connecting theological education, community engagement, and leadership development. His professional experience includes building partnerships with faith-based organizations, developing community-centered programs, and supporting clergy serving historically underserved communities.
Dr. Smith also serves as a pastor and has contributed to projects involving Black faith leadership, community development, and the preservation of religious and civil rights history.
His leadership in the RELI Clergy Wellness Initiative reflects a commitment to ensuring that clergy receive the resources, encouragement, and institutional support necessary to sustain their ministries.



Rev. Dr. James D. Foster, Leadership Coach and Spiritual Advisor


Rev. Dr. James D. Foster, PhD, MDiv, is a theologian, pastor, author, and leadership coach whose professional work focuses on strengthening faith-based leadership and organizational effectiveness.
His experience includes pastoral ministry, theological education, leadership development, and coaching for mission-driven organizations.
As the initiative’s Certified Leadership Coach and Spiritual Advisor, Dr. Foster contributes expertise in spiritual formation, leadership resilience, personal development, and the challenges associated with sustaining effective ministry.
His perspective reinforces the importance of connecting professional leadership growth with personal reflection, spiritual well-being, and long-term vocational purpose.



Larry Love, Wellness and Performance Coach


Larry Love, MS, AT, ATC, CSC, is a wellness and performance professional whose work emphasizes physical health, movement, personal wellness, and sustainable lifestyle practices.
Through Total Body Wellness & Performance, Love has provided wellness education tailored to individuals whose professional responsibilities can make consistent self-care challenging.
His work with faith leaders emphasizes the importance of attending to physical health while managing the demands of caregiving and ministry.
As Wellness and Performance Coach, Love brings an applied health and wellness perspective to the RELI team, helping connect the initiative’s broader mission of clergy resilience with practical approaches to physical well-being.



Christian Horn, Healthcare Technology Founder and Statistician


Christian Horn, BBA, is a healthcare technology entrepreneur whose professional interests include digital innovation, data-informed decision-making, and the application of technology to health and wellness.
Identified in the RELI evaluation report as an investor and founder of DYMND.AI, Horn brings a technology and business perspective to the multidisciplinary initiative.
His inclusion on the team reflects the potential role of digital tools, data systems, and technology-enabled monitoring in supporting wellness programming and program evaluation.
Within the broader context of RELI, this expertise complements the pastoral, coaching, and public health perspectives represented by other team members.



Chloe A. Smith, Public Health and Data Strategist and Program Coordinator


Chloe A. Smith, BSPH, is a public health professional and Master of Public Health candidate at Morehouse School of Medicine, with experience in program coordination, community engagement, evaluation, and data visualization.
Her work spans public health research, organizational programming, stakeholder engagement, and the translation of health information into accessible communication products.
Through her work with Chicago Theological Seminary, Smith has supported clergy wellness programming through coordination, evaluation-related activities, and the integration of public health perspectives into faith-based initiatives.
Her contributions to Beyond the Pulpit reflect an interest in connecting public health practice with faith institutions, using data storytelling to communicate program experiences and inform future opportunities for health promotion.

title: About the Initiative
section: A Multidisciplinary Approach to Clergy Wellness
text:
A Multidisciplinary Approach to Clergy Wellness
The RELI team brings together five complementary areas of expertise:

Faith and community leadership: Connecting clergy wellness to the broader mission of sustainable ministry.
Spiritual formation and leadership coaching: Supporting reflection, personal development, and vocational resilience.
Physical wellness and performance: Emphasizing movement, health education, and sustainable self-care.
Healthcare technology and data: Exploring opportunities to support wellness monitoring and information management.
Public health and program evaluation: Translating program information into evidence that can inform communication and future planning.

Together, these perspectives illustrate why clergy wellness extends beyond any single discipline.
